qs.q: A 45-year-old patient with an invasive fungal infection is started on amphotericin B. Renal function tests a week later show a rise in serum creatinine and a drop in creatinine clearance. What is the primary mechanism of this drug-induced nephrotoxicity?
o: Direct tubular cell lysis coupled with intense vasoconstriction
Immune-mediated interstitial nephritis driven by lymphocytes
Precipitation of insoluble drug crystals inside the lumen
Inhibition of glomerular prostaglandin synthesis for ischemia
Irreversible covalent binding to the basement membrane
qs.e: Amphotericin B binds ergosterol in renal tubular membranes, forming pores and causing vasoconstriction that reduces GFR.

qs.q: A patient presents with hemoptysis, iron deficiency anemia, and pulmonary infiltrates. Renal function tests are completely normal, and anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies are absent. Which diagnosis best fits these findings?
qs.e: Idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis presents with pulmonary findings similar to Goodpasture syndrome but lacks renal disease and anti-GBM antibodies. Goodpasture syndrome is explicitly defined by the presence of renal disease and anti-GBM antibodies.

ai.title: Renal Function Tests
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Renal function tests assess glomerular filtration and tubular handling to detect acute or chronic kidney injury. In low‑resource settings clinicians must interpret limited results and know alternatives when assays are unavailable.

sections.p: Renal function tests are laboratory measurements that estimate glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and identify disturbances in urea, creatinine, electrolytes and acid‑base balance.
b: Serum creatinine reflects GFR; rises when GFR falls below ~60 mL/min/1.73 m².
Blood urea nitrogen (BUN) rises with reduced clearance or high protein catabolism.
Electrolytes (Na+, K+, HCO3‑) reveal tubular dysfunction.

sections.p: Kidney disease is staged by estimated GFR (eGFR) using the CKD‑EPI or MDRD equation, adjusted for African ethnicity when possible.
b: Stage 1: eGFR ≥90 with evidence of kidney damage.
Stage 2: eGFR 60–89.
Stage 3a: eGFR 45–59; 3b: 30–44.
Stage 4: eGFR 15–29.
Stage 5: eGFR <15 (kidney failure).

sections.p: In East African hospitals the common precipitants of abnormal renal tests are infections, volume depletion and drug toxicity.
b: Infectious: severe malaria, sepsis, HIV‑associated nephropathy, TB meningitis.
Volume‑related: diarrhoea, vomiting, diuretic over‑use.
Nephrotoxic drugs: aminoglycosides, amphotericin B, traditional herbal remedies.
Obstructive: schistosomiasis‑related ureteric strictures, stones.

sections.p: Patients may have oliguria, edema, fatigue, nausea, or be asymptomatic with only laboratory derangement.
b: Reduced urine output (<400 mL/24 h) suggests acute kidney injury.
Peripheral edema and pulmonary crackles indicate fluid overload.
Metabolic acidosis (low HCO3‑) causes rapid breathing.

t.b: What is the current GFR? – Elevated creatinine indicates reduced filtration; calculate eGFR for staging.
Is there impaired clearance or high catabolism? – High BUN with high creatinine confirms renal dysfunction; a high BUN/creatinine ratio (>20:1) suggests pre‑renal causes.
Are tubular functions disturbed? – Hyperkalaemia warns of imminent cardiac arrhythmia; low HCO3‑ signals metabolic acidosis.
Is there protein, haematuria or infection? – Proteinuria >1 g/day suggests glomerular disease; granular casts point to acute tubular necrosis.
Can we quickly assess renal function? – Gives an approximate creatinine; if markedly elevated, treat as AKI while arranging formal labs.

sections.p: Unrecognised renal failure can rapidly progress to life‑threatening complications.
b: Severe hyperkalaemia (>6.0 mmol/L) → ventricular arrhythmia.
Pulmonary oedema with hypoxia.
Uremic encephalopathy (confusion, asterixis).
Acute metabolic acidosis (pH <7.30).

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, protect remaining kidney function and correct metabolic derangements.
b: Rehydrate cautiously in pre‑renal AKI; avoid fluid overload.
Stop nephrotoxic drugs; substitute with safer alternatives (e.g., use fluconazole instead of amphotericin B when possible).
Administer loop diuretics for volume overload only after assessing volume status.
Correct hyperkalaemia with calcium gluconate, insulin‑glucose, or sodium bicarbonate.
Consider renal replacement therapy if refractory hyperkalaemia, severe acidosis, or fluid overload.

sections.p: Serial monitoring guides recovery and prevents chronic kidney disease.
b: Repeat creatinine and electrolytes every 24–48 h in AKI.
Educate patients on avoiding NSAIDs, herbal nephrotoxins, and maintaining hydration.
Screen for HIV, hepatitis B/C and control blood pressure to reduce CKD progression.

sections.p: Renal function tests are sometimes mistaken for liver function tests or for a full metabolic panel.
b: Liver function tests assess transaminases, bilirubin, not GFR.
Electrolyte panels without creatinine do not estimate filtration.
Low muscle mass (malnutrition, chronic illness) may mask high creatinine; use cystatin C if available.
High protein diet or gastrointestinal bleeding raises BUN without renal injury.
Severe hyperglycaemia can cause pseudohyponatraemia.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly falling urine output (<0.5 mL/kg/h for >6 h)

faq.q: Why is creatinine preferred over BUN for estimating GFR?
faq.a: Creatinine is produced at a relatively constant rate and cleared mainly by glomerular filtration, whereas BUN is affected by diet, catabolism and hydration.

faq.q: Can a normal creatinine rule out kidney injury?
faq.a: No; early AKI or low muscle mass can keep creatinine normal. Look at urine output and trends.

faq.q: What if the laboratory cannot measure electrolytes?
faq.a: Use bedside dipstick for potassium and bicarbonate, and clinical signs (muscle weakness, arrhythmia) to guide urgent treatment.

exam: A patient with severe malaria develops oliguria and a creatinine rise from 0.9 to 2.4 mg/dL – what is the next immediate management step? — Assess volume status, give cautious fluid bolus if hypovolaemic, stop nephrotoxic drugs, and monitor electrolytes.

How does a BUN/creatinine ratio >20:1 help differentiate pre‑renal from intrinsic AKI? — It suggests reduced renal perfusion with preserved filtration, prompting fluid resuscitation rather than dialysis.
Why is hyperkalaemia more dangerous than hypernatremia in acute kidney injury? — Potassium directly affects cardiac membrane potential, causing life‑threatening arrhythmias.

A patient on amphotericin B shows rising creatinine; what alternative antifungal could be used in a low‑resource setting and why? — Fluconazole, because it is less nephrotoxic and does not require intensive monitoring.
Explain how schistosomiasis can lead to chronic renal impairment. — Egg‑induced granulomas cause ureteric obstruction and hydronephrosis, eventually reducing GFR.
What are the limitations of using eGFR equations in African patients with low muscle mass? — They may underestimate true GFR; clinicians should rely on trends and urine output.

When is renal replacement therapy indicated in AKI despite optimal medical management? — Persistent hyperkalaemia >6.0 mmol/L, refractory acidosis (pH <7.20), or fluid overload unresponsive to diuretics.
Distinguish the urine findings in acute tubular necrosis versus glomerulonephritis. — ATN shows muddy brown granular casts; GN shows dysmorphic RBCs and red cell casts.
